name: Computed Tomography Perfusion
domain-match_rationale: CTP can identify areas of abnormal cerebral perfusion that may be strongly associated with Delayed Cerebral Ischemia. However, it is not a direct measure of DCI and it does not assess signs of neurological impairment.
feasibility_rationale: CTP is generally feasible across aSAH treatment centres, but it exposes patients to radiation,  critically ill patients need to be transported to the CTP scanner, and it requires expertise to use and interpret.
description: Computed tomography perfusion (CTP) is an imaging technique that allows clinicians to assess how blood flows through the brain. It works by taking a rapid series of CT scans as an intravenous injection of iodine-based contrast material passes through the cerebral circulation. The images are processed by a computer to measure and generate maps of cerebral perfusion. Following aSAH, CTP can be used to identify areas of abnormal cerebral perfusion, such as reduced cerebral blood flow (CBF) or increased mean transit time (MTT), that may be associated with Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Cremers CHP, van der Schaaf IC, Wensink E, et al. CT Perfusion and Delayed Cerebral Ischemia in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. J Cereb Blood Flow Metab 2014; 34(2): 200–07. https://doi.org/10.1038/jcbfm.2013.208
reference_2: Sun H, Ma J, Liu Y, You C. CT Perfusion for Identification of Patients at Risk for Delayed Cerebral Ischemia during the Acute Phase after Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Meta-analysis. Neurol India 2019; 67(5): 1235-1239. https://doi.org/10.4103/0028-3886.271235

name: Clinical Examination
domain-match_rationale: Clinical examination can assess the occurrence of focal neurological impairment (such as hemiparesis, aphasia, apraxia, hemianopia, or neglect), central to the consensus definition. However, it is limited in determining DCI as the cause of observed changes.
feasibility_rationale: Neurological/Clinical examination is feasible when a patient is concious and alert; however, examination cannot be done when a patient is unconcious, sedated, intubated, etc.
description: Neurological or clinical examination after aSAH involves regularly assessing a patient for changes such as a new or worsening weakness, difficulty speaking, confusion, or a decrease in level of consciousness. Changes that cannot be explained by another cause may indicate the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia (DCI).

name: Electroencephalogram
domain-match_rationale: Electroencephalogram (EEG) can monitor for changes in brain activity that may associated with the development of DCI; however, observed changes may be due to other causes, requiring interpretation and clinical judgement.
feasibility_rationale: EEG availability may be limited ascross centres, patient sedation must be reduced, and EEG must be continuously read by a trained expert.
description: Electroencephalography (EEG) uses electrodes placed on the scalp to record the brain’s electrical activity. Continuous EEG (cEEG) records this activity over an extended period, allowing changes in brain-wave patterns to be monitored over time. Quantitative EEG (qEEG) uses mathematical methods, such as Fourier transformation, to process the raw EEG signal into quantitative measures that can be displayed as graphs or trends, making changes easier to identify. Following aSAH, continuous EEG, with or without qEEG analysis, can be used to identify changes in the brain’s electrical activity that may be associated with the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Rots ML, van Putten MJAM, Hoedemaekers CWE, et al. Continuous EEG Monitoring for Early Detection of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia in Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A Pilot Study. Neurocritical Care 2016; 24(2): 207–16. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12028-015-0205-y
reference_2:
Claassen J, Hirsch LJ, Kreiter KT, et al. Quantitative continuous EEG for detecting delayed cerebral ischemia in patients with poor-grade subarachnoid hemorrhage. 
Clinical Neurophysiology 2004; 2699-2710,

name: Cerebral Microdialysis
domain-match_rationale: Cerebral Microdialysis can provide continuous monitoring for changes in brain fluid composition that may be associated with developing DCI. However, it is not a direct measure of DCI, since these changes may be due to other causes. The probe also samples only a small region, which may not be representative of the entire brain.
feasibility_rationale: Cerebral Microdialysis has limited availability across treatment centres, requires complex and invasive catheter placement, and requires continuous monitoring of results by a trained expert.
description: Cerebral microdialysis is an invasive technique that uses a small probe placed into the brain to monitor changes in brain fluid chemistry. Following aSAH, changes in the chemistry of the brain tissue around the probe may indicate that the tissue is not getting or using energy normally, which could signal the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia (DCI).

name: Invasive Oxygen Pressure Monitoring
domain-match_rationale: Invasive Oxygen Pressure Monitoring (PbtO2) can monitor for changes in brain tissue oxygenation, which may be associated with DCI. However, observed changes may be due to other causes and the probe samples a small region which may not be representative of the entire brain.
feasibility_rationale: PbtO2 has limited availability across treatment centres, requires complex and invasive probe placement, and requires continuous monitoring by a trained expert. Another issue is that not all PbtO2 monitors are MRI compatible; while this is not necessarily a problem for DCI specifically, it could affect assessment/treatment options available for adressing other aSAH related complications.
description: Invasive oxygen pressure monitoring (PbtO2) uses a small probe placed into the brain to continuously measure the amount of oxygen available in the surrounding brain tissue. Following aSAH, a decrease in brain tissue oxygen levels could signal the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia (DCI).

name: Non-Contrast Computed Tomography
domain-match_rationale: Non-contrast CT can help determine whether a patient has developed a cerebral infarction that may be attributable to Delayed Cerebral Ischemia. However, since CT primarily detects irreversibly injured or infarcted tissue, it is best suited to post-DCI assessments, and when paired with information about the clinical context.
feasibility_rationale: CT is widely available and routine across centres. The primary feasibility concerns are radiation exposure and transportation of a critically ill patient.
description: Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) is an X-ray imaging technique performed without intravenous contrast material. Cerebral infarction can appear on these images as an area of reduced tissue density. Following aSAH, non-contrast CT can be used to determine whether a patient has developed a cerebral infarction that may be attributable to Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Vergouwen MDI, Vermeulen M, van Gijn J, et al. Definition of delayed cerebral ischemia after aneurysmal sub-arachnoid hemorrhage as an outcome event in clinical trials and observational studies: proposal of a multidisciplinary research group. Stroke 2010; 41: 2391–5.

name: Transcranial Doppler Techniques
domain-match_rationale: Transcranial Doppler Techniques provide an indirect measure of vasospasm, rather than a direct measure of DCI.
description: Transcranial Doppler (TCD) is a non-invasive ultrasound technique that measures blood-flow velocity in the major arteries within the brain. The TCD probe is placed over specific areas of the patient’s head. The probe transmits sound waves into the cerebral arteries, which are reflected by moving red blood cells. The change in frequency between the emitted and reflected waves, referred to as the “Doppler shift frequency", is used to calculate the velocity of moving blood. Increasing blood-flow velocities can indicate narrowing of an artery. Following aSAH, TCD can be used to monitor changes in cerebral blood-flow velocities, which may identify vasospasm and help predict the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Purkayastha S, and Sorond F. Transcranial Doppler Ultrasound: Technique and Application. Semin Neurol 2012; 32(4): 411–20. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0032-1331812

name: Near-Infrared Spectroscopy
domain-match_rationale: Near-infrared spectroscopy measures regional oxygenation of brain tissue, rather than providing a direct measure of DCI.
description: Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) is a non-invasive monitoring technique which uses near-infrared light to estimate oxygenation of brain tissue.  Sensors are placed on the patient’s head and emit near-infrared light. As the light that passes through brain tissue, it is absorbed differently by oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin, allowing clinicians to estimate regional brain oxygenation. Following aSAH, a decrease in regional brain oxygenation may indicate reduced cerebral blood flow or oxygen delivery and help predict the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Park JJ, Kim C, Jeon JP. Monitoring of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia in Patients with Subarachnoid Hemorrhage via Near-Infrared Spectroscopy. J Clin Med 2020; 9(5):1595. https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm9051595

name: CT Angiography
domain-match_rationale: CT Angiography (CTA) is an instrument used to detect vasospasm, rather than DCI.
description: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) is an imaging technique that is used to capture detailed images of blood vessels that can show areas of narrowing. It works by taking a series of computed tomography (CT) scans as an iodinated contrast material is injected intravenously and passes through the cerebral circulation. The images are then processed by a computer. Following aSAH, CTA can be used to identify cerebral vasospasm, which may be associated with the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Dankbaar JW, de Rooij NK, Velthuis, BK, et al. Diagnosing Delayed Cerebral Ischemia With Different CT Modalities in Patients With Subarachnoid Hemorrhage With Clinical Deterioration. Stroke 2009; 40(11): 3493-3498. https://doi.org/10.1161/STROKEAHA.109.559013

name: Bispectral Index Monitoring
domain-match_rationale: Bispectral Index (BIS) monitoring measures the brain's electrical activity, rather than being a direct measure of DCI. Observed changes in a patient's BIS value may help predict DCI, but there is currently limited evidence available and further validation is needed to support its use for DCI.
description: Bispectral index (BIS) monitoring is a non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) technique that uses electrodes placed on the patient’s forehead to record electrical activity from the brain. The EEG signal is processed into a numerical BIS value ranges from 0, indicating very low or absent detectable brain inactivity, to 100, indicating a fully awake and alert state. Following aSAH, BIS has been investigated as a non-invasive bedside tool for monitoring decreased in the brain’s electrical activity that may be associated with the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Hernández-Hernández MA, Cherchi MS, Torres-Díez E, et al. Bispectral Index Monitoring to Detect Delayed Cerebral Ischemia after Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. Journal of Critical Care 2022; 72. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcrc.2022.154154

name: Digital Subtraction Angiography
domain-match_rationale: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) is an instrument used to detect vasospasm, rather than DCI directly.
description: Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is an imaging technique used to obtain detailed images of cerebral blood vessels. It involves taking an initial X-ray image, and then taking a series of X-ray images as an iodinated contrast material is injected. A computer processes the images and subtracts background structures such as bone so that the blood vessels can be clearly visualized. Following aSAH, DSA can be used to identify arterial narrowing that may be associated with the development of Delayed Cerebral Ischemia.
reference_1: Glick Y, Balasubramanian S, Zheng A, et al. Digital subtraction angiography. Radiopaedia.org. Available online [Accessed on 17 Jun 2026]: https://doi.org/10.53347/rID-62028

name: Definition Frameworks
domain-match_rationale: Definition Frameworks are nonspecific. Often, these combine reference standards and sets of criteria that are not exclusive to DCI, making it difficult to disentangle DCI from Cerebral Infarction.
description: Definition frameworks are standardized sets of criteria and reference standards used to determine whether an event following aSAH should be classified as Delayed Cerebral Ischemia (DCI). Definition frameworks are intended to improve consistency in how DCI events are classified across patients, observers, and studies.
reference_1: Zafar SF, Westover MB, Gaspard N, et al. Interrater Agreement for Consensus Definitions of Delayed Ischemic Events After Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. Journal of Clinical Neurophysiology 2016; 33(3): 235–40. https://doi.org/10.1097/WNP.0000000000000276
reference_2: Sanelli PC, Anumula N, Gold R, et al. Outcomes-Based Assessment of a New Reference Standard for Delayed Cerebral Ischemia Related to Vasospasm in Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage. Academic Radiology 2012; 19(9): 1066–74. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.acra.2012.04.010

name: Multimodal and Longitudinal Monitoring
domain-match_rationale: Multimodal and Longitudinal monitoring has potential to be a strong candidate for the COS, but the exact modalities and monitoring schedule needs to be defined before it can be assessed as an instrument.
